column1: # tests/budgets.tsv - Q6: performance budgets, and where each came from.
# One row per measurement the kernel emits as a `[perf] name value unit`
# line. tools/qemu-serial-test.sh reads this and fails the run when a
# measurement exceeds its ceiling.
# Every number here is a CEILING with stated headroom over a MEASURED
# value, in the same discipline SECONDS_TO_RUN's comment history in
# qemu-serial-test.sh already applies to itself. The `measured` and
# `commit` columns are what make a failure diagnosable: "the disk got
# three times slower since b7bb520" is a starting point, "too slow" is
# not.
# A budget that has sat at 2x slack for ten milestones is a bug in the
# budget. Re-measure and tighten it, and say so here when you do.
# These were measured on QEMU under macOS on Apple Silicon. There is no
# hosted runner behind them and there is not meant to be one: they are a
# claim about this machine. Measured somewhere else they will move, and
# moving them with a recorded reason is the process working.
# Q18: the `input_to_photon_*_{best,med,worst}` rows replaced a single
# number that swung 3x between consecutive runs of the same image. The
# `measured` column for those six is now a real observation, and the
# first one taught something the single number could not: within one
# boot the idle path is tight (40757 / 42303 / 43475 us - a 7% spread),
# while the loaded worst frame is twice the loaded median (81547 against
# 40742). So the 3x swing that motivated this milestone was *between*
# boots, not within one, and it is the boot conditions that vary rather
# than the path. That is a different problem, it is now visible, and it
# is what these rows exist to keep visible.
# name<TAB>ceiling<TAB>unit<TAB>measured<TAB>commit<TAB>note
boot_to_desktop_s
column6: The full self-test boot. Dominated by tests that spawn a process and wait for it, so it is variable rather than merely large - the ceiling is set against a busy host, not a quiet one. An ordinary boot with self-tests off is ~8s and is not this number. M102 moved the measured value from 192 s to 223 s on purpose: its self-test exhausts the machine's physical memory twice, and on the 4 GiB configuration that is about a million page faults per round. The ceiling did not move - there is still most of it spare - but the measured column has to say what a run now costs, or the next person to add thirty seconds will think they added five.

column1: disk_1mib_cold_us
column6: 1 MiB through virtio-blk, cache dropped first. The README quotes 5.6 ms for virtio and 95 ms for the ATA PIO fallback; the ceiling covers both paths plus headroom, because QEMU_DISK=ide runs the same marker.

column1: disk_1mib_warm_us
column6: The same megabyte out of M92's write-through cache. Generous headroom on purpose: this is a memcpy whose cost is dominated by whatever else the host is doing.

column1: input_to_photon_idle_us
column6: Cursor motion to a changed pixel, TSC-measured, on an idle machine. M69's own note says the observer competes, so this is an upper bound rather than a measurement of the path alone.

column1: input_to_photon_loaded_us
column6: The same, with CPU-bound tasks running. The number that matters for "does the desktop stay usable under load", and the one most sensitive to the host.

column1: input_to_photon_idle_best_us
column6: Q18: the shape rather than a sample. The best case is what the path costs when nothing is in the way.

column1: input_to_photon_idle_med_us
column6: Q18: what it usually costs. This is the row a regression in the ordinary path moves.

column1: input_to_photon_idle_worst_us
column6: Q18: what a person actually notices. A desktop is judged by its worst frames, so this is the row with an opinion in it.

column1: input_to_photon_loaded_best_us
column6: Q18: as above, with CPU-bound tasks running.

column1: input_to_photon_loaded_med_us
input_to_photon_loaded_worst_us
column6: Q18: the worst frame under load, which is the number that decides whether the desktop stays usable. Deliberately the widest here: it is also the noisiest, and a different host will move it.

column1: syscall_null_cycles
column6: M101: what one `int 0x80` round trip costs, measured with SYS_getpid - a call that does almost nothing, so what is left is the trap, the dispatch and the return. This is the number the `syscall`/`sysret` deferral has been waiting for since M69. The ceiling is ~4x a measurement that moved between 1020 and 1300 cycles across three boots of the same image, because it is a cycle count taken on a virtualised TSC and it is the noisiest row here; what it is for is catching a trap path that has become an order of magnitude slower, not policing jitter.

column1: disk_1mib_write_absorbed_us
column6: M104: 1 MiB written block by block into the writeback cache and then barriered to the disk. The ceiling is the same as the cold READ's, because the write path can never be cheaper than the read it is measured against and this is a regression ceiling rather than a target.

column1: disk_1mib_write_through_us
column6: M104: the same megabyte a sector at a time, which is the write-through path. Kept as a row because it is the denominator of the writeback ratio - a run where these two converge is a run where writeback stopped absorbing anything, and that is the regression this catches.

column1: disk_1mib_seq_read_no_readahead_us
column6: M104: 1 MiB read sequentially with readahead off, which is the default. The pair below is the measurement that chose that default.

column1: disk_1mib_seq_read_readahead_us
column6: M104: the same read with eight lines fetched ahead. Slower, and the row exists so that the day it stops being slower - a smaller filesystem block, a device where a byte costs more than a request - the number says so rather than somebody arguing about it.

column1: mount_scan_us
column6: M105: the full scan an unclean mount runs - every allocated inode's block tree walked, a shadow bitmap built, the two compared - over the ordinary boot filesystem, with the block cache dropped first. Cold on purpose: a mount scan runs because the machine was NOT shut down cleanly, so it always runs on a just-booted machine. Measured warm the same scan swung 4747 to 25476 us across two boots, which is a measurement of the run before it. This is the row M71's second condition - "a full scan gets slow" - is decided by, and the ceiling is an opinion rather than headroom: 100 ms is where a mount stops being instant and becomes a wait, which is the point at which a journal would be worth building.

column1: mount_scan_busy_us
column6: M105: the same scan after four concurrent writers have added and deleted several hundred files. Same ceiling, and the pair is the measurement: the number does not move with the file count, because the cost is a pass over the resident inode table rather than a walk of the tree. That is the structural reason the deferral holds, and this row is what would stop being true the day the inode table stops being resident.

column1: four_writers_us
column6: M105: four processes creating, writing, fsyncing, renaming and deleting concurrently through one coarse filesystem lock. Wide on purpose - it is four processes on a virtualised disk and it moved 267 ms to 321 ms across three boots. What it guards is not throughput but liveness: a change that makes two writers serialise pathologically, or deadlock, shows up here as a run that never finishes rather than as a slow one.
